Where the two ontologies part: a property the write path stamps that the
primary ontology does not declare, or one the primary ontology declares that

recorded in `chunks`, which the primary ontology has no need of because a
record does not cite a passage. Nor is its collapse, which the shortcut holds.

A relationship asserts that a claim exists and what identifies it — nothing
more. The properties it declares, and only those, are its **Claim Key**: they
are normalized and form the edge's merge key, because the relationship means
something different at a different value — two articles naming different
amounts assert different things and get separate edges. Anything else an
article said about the relationship stays in the `Chunk` the edge points back
to. A Claim Key property is not required of the extractor: an edge that
arrives without one is written and carries `needs_review`.

## Divergences from the primary ontology

Where the two ontologies part: a property the write path stamps that the
primary ontology does not declare, or one the primary ontology declares that
news cannot supply. Either way it marks something nothing we hold can settle.
Unlike a shortcut, a divergence is not reversible from our own record: closing
one needs an authoritative source.

An edge's evidence is not a divergence: the `Chunk` it was read from is
recorded in `chunks`, which the primary ontology has no need of because a
record does not cite a passage. Nor is its collapse, which the shortcut holds.

The gap column is derived, not declared: a property the primary ontology
declares is one news drops, and one it does not declare is one the write
path stamps. Nothing records the direction twice.

| Property | Applies to | Gap | Why it diverges |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `Bill` / `Campaign` / `Committee` / `LegislativeEvent` / `Organization` / `Politician` / `Prop` | news cannot supply it | A node's key is minted by the write path from its label and the name the article used, so that two articles naming one entity reach one node. A single article cannot see that agreement, so an extractor supplying an `id` would be keying the graph off prose it alone read. |
| `name` | `Campaign` / `Committee` / `Organization` | news cannot supply it | The extractor already reports the surface string as the entity's name, and the write path copies it into the properties itself. Asking for it twice invites a second, different spelling of the same name. |
| `first_name` | `Politician` | news cannot supply it | Splitting a person's name is entity resolution, not extraction. Whether `Anamarie Avila Farias` surnames as `Farias` or `Avila Farias` is not something the chunk states, and only an authoritative roster settles it. |
| `last_name` | `Politician` | news cannot supply it | The other half of the same split, and unresolvable for the same reason: a chunk names a person, it does not parse them. |
| `name` | `LegislativeEvent` / `Politician` / `Prop` | the write path stamps it | The extractor identifies an entity by the surface string the article used, but these labels declare structured fields instead of a `name`. Only entity resolution against an authoritative record can populate them. |
| `session_verified` | `Bill` | the write path stamps it | A `Bill` id is only stable per legislative session, and news prose rarely names one. Tier 1 resolves it from a linked authoritative bill page, so the session is as good as the source and the key is final. |
| `name` | `Bill` | news cannot supply it | A `Bill`'s name is its Bill Designation, parsed from the surface string the article used and supplied by Bill Session Resolution. The extraction model reports only that surface string, so it must not guess or decompose the designation itself. |
| `session_inferred` | `Bill` | the write path stamps it | Tier 2 guesses the session from the article's publication date, which is wrong for a bill discussed outside the session that introduced it. The key is provisional: only the authoritative session can confirm or re-key it. |
| `date_verified` | `LegislativeEvent` | the write path stamps it | The article stated the date of the event, so the `date` is as good as the source. It is still not part of the key: the date identifies nothing here, it is the fact a later reconciliation joins on. |
| `date_inferred` | `LegislativeEvent` | the write path stamps it | The article dated the event no other way, so its publication date stands in. News usually reports an event within a day or two of it happening, which makes the stand-in near enough to join on and far too soft to key on. |
| `sequence_number` | `LegislativeEvent` | news cannot supply it | An article reports that a hearing or a vote happened, never where it sat among the events before it. A single article sees one event, so nothing we hold can order it against another article's, and only an authoritative legislative record supplies the position. |
| `needs_review` | `Bill` / `LegislativeEvent` | the write path stamps it | For a `Bill`, no session could be resolved or inferred, so the key is a placeholder that nothing we hold can settle. For a `LegislativeEvent`, neither the article nor its metadata yielded a date, so the event carries none and a later reconciliation has nothing to join on. |
| `transaction_id` | `FUNDED` | news cannot supply it | An article reports that money moved, never the FPPC filing that recorded it. Nothing an article carries identifies the transaction, and only the disclosure record itself supplies the id. |
| `needs_review` | `DECLARED_STANCE` / `FUNDED` | the write path stamps it | The article asserted the relationship without a value the claim depends on, or named one in a form nothing else will match. The edge is real but its key is incomplete, so it cannot yet be compared against another article's. |
